newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Renault adds French cuts to Belgian.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Renault adds French cuts to Belgian.

text.p: French carmakers Renault SA, battling big losses, a price war and shrinking demand, told its workforce on Tuesday it plans to axe 2,764 jobs in France this year on top of a fiercely disputed plant closure in Belgium.

The French government defended the privatised company's need to restructure to survive stiff competition, but urged Renault's management to open talks with the French and Belgian authorities and with trade unions on limiting the human impact of the plan.
He raised the prospect of public money to cushion the blow.
The job cuts caused anger in the French parliament and union leaders warned Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer he could face a long labour conflict.

The plan to axe jobs in France follows last Thursday's abrupt decision to close the Renault plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels in June, with the loss of 3,100 direct jobs and another 1,000 more at risk at supplying companies.
It was contained in information handed out to works council members ahead of a meeting with management on Thursday, union sources said. Renault has a total workforce of 140,000.

In Brussels, Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene met union leaders from Vilvoorde, his home town, and said emotions were running so high over the plant closure that he could not rule out a boycott of Renault cars by the Belgian public.

Schweitzer told reporters at the Geneva Car Show that closing Vilvoorde was an industrial necessity and it would have been dishonest to conduct a phoney negotiation on the "grave and painful" decision.
In Paris, Industry Minister Franck Borotra faced angry questions not only from the Socialist and Communist opposition but also from President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR party.
He said the government had not been involved or consulted in the decision by the "independent" management of Renault, in which the state still has a 46 percent stake and boardroom seats.

But Renault, Europe's sixth biggest car maker, had to cut costs if it was to survive, the minister said. The company is expected to announce this month a 1996 operating loss of up to three billion francs ($520.5 million) plus heavy charges for restructuring.
"Companies that are not able to face competition are in the end companies that will disappear," Borotra said.
He said that at Prime Minister Alain Juppe's request, he was urging Renault to renew talks with the authorities about financing the job reduction plan.

Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin called the Vilvoorde closure "financially, industrially and socially absurd", tarnishing France's social image in Europe. The company had only recently spent 1.4 billion francs on modernising the plant.
A Renault spokeswoman said the central works council would meet on March 13 to discuss an "employment plan" in France.
The planned cuts are the biggest since the company shed 3,700 jobs in 1992 when still state-owned.
Renault unions have called a one-hour strike on Friday in all plants in France, Belgium and Spain to protest against the shutdown of the Belgian factory.
"We hope this is the beginning of a long period of labour struggle at Renault all over Europe," Daniel Richter of the pro-Socialist CFDT union said on Europe 1 radio.

Borotra told parliament the government had rejected a joint proposal by Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen to retire 40,000 older car workers and recruit 14,000 young job-seekers because it would have cost taxpayers 40 billion francs and undermined government policy on early retirement.

The Flanders regional government has said it will sue Renault for allegedly failing to respect European labour law over the closure of Vilvoorde. But a senior Renault executive said he saw no legal basis.
"We have completely respected all the procedures," Michel de Virville, senior vice-president in charge of personnel and external relations, told reporters in Geneva.

General Motors, the world's biggest carmaker, said that job losses at Renault and Ford signalled the start of a long awaited shakeout in Europe, but it hoped to avoid similar action. ($ = 5.763 French Francs)
